title: Supreme Court clears the way for nuclear waste storage - NewsBreak
text: WASHINGTON (NEXSTAR) – The Supreme Court in a 6-3 ruling cleared the way for a West Texas facility to store nuclear waste on Wednesday. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, writing for the court, said Texas didn’t have the right to sue to stop the Nuclear Regulatory Commission from issuing a temporary license for spent nuclear fuel storage. “It’s very stable, very safe, stored inside some very robust containers,” said Steve Nesbit, a nuclear engineer and nuclear safety analyst. “The storage of spent fuel has never harmed anyone.” The high court did not consider Texas’ underlying argument. Texas said the federal government can’t license a private location, offsite from a nuclear plant, to store nuclear waste. Justice Neil Gorsuch said in his dissent, federal law only allows the storage of spent nuclear fuel “at a nuclear reactor or a federally owned facility.” The federal government licensed the site for temporary storage. Texas sued and the case ended up at the Supreme Court. “If anyone thinks this is temporary, I have a bridge to sell you,” said Texas Solicitor General Aaron Nielson in oral arguments in March. “What the commission has just done is put a permanent terrorist bullseye on the most productive oil field in America. The spent nuclear fuel would be stored over the Permian Basin. But Nesbit said spent fuel is very safe. “Most of the radioactivity has decayed off. There’s not a lot of heat there,” he said. In 1982, Congress passed the Nuclear Waste Policy Act. It said it’s the federal government’s responsibility to find a permanent place to store the nation’s spent nuclear fuel. Federal authorities initially selected Yucca Mountain, Northwest of Las Vegas. The project stalled because of opposition. 43 years later, the government hasn’t found another permanent location. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission said temporary storage sites are needed because nuclear plants are running out of room, or some nuclear sites are decommissioned, but still hold spent nuclear fuel. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to WGN-TV.
